title: Jesus and the sorcerers
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις ὁ Κέλσος ὑπιδόμενος τὰ ἐπιδειχθησόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ γεγενημένα μεγάλα, περὶ ὧν ὀλίγα ἀπὸ πολλῶν εἰρήκαμεν, προσποιεῖται συγχωρεῖν ἀληθῆ εἶναι ὅσα περὶ θεραπειῶν ἢ ἀναστάσεως ἢ περὶ ἄρτων ὀλίγων θρεψάντων πολλοὺς ἀναγέγραπται, ἀφ᾿ ὧν λείψανα πολλὰ καταλέλειπται, ἢ ὅσα ἄλλα οἴεται τερατευσαμένους τοὺς μαθητὰς ἱστορηκέναι, καὶ ἐπιφέρει αὐτοῖς· φέρε πιστεύσωμεν εἶναί σοι ταῦτ᾿ εἰργασμένα. καὶ εὐθέως κοινοποιεῖ αὐτὰ πρὸς τὰ ἔργα τῶν γοήτων, ὡς ὑπισχνουμένων θαυμασιώτερα, καὶ πρὸς τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν μαθόντων ἀπὸ Αἰγυπτίων ἐπιτελούμενα, ἐν μέσαις ἀγοραῖς ὀλίγων ὀβολῶν ἀποδομένων τὰ σεμνὰ μαθήματα καὶ δαίμονας ἀπὸ ἀνθρώπων ἐξελαυνόντων καὶ νόσους ἀποφυσώντων καὶ ψυχὰς ἡρώων ἀνακαλούντων δεῖπνά τε πολυτελῆ καὶ τραπέζας καὶ πέμματα καὶ ὄψα τὰ οὐκ ὄντα δεικνύντων καὶ ὡς ζῷα κινούντων οὐκ ἀληθῶς ὄντα ζῷα ἀλλὰ μέχρι φαντασίας φαινόμενα τοιαῦτα, καὶ φησιν· ἆρ᾿ ἐπεὶ ταῦτα ποιοῦσιν ἐκεῖνοι, δεήσει ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς ἡγεῖσθαι υἱοὺς εἶναι θεοῦ; ἢ λεκτέον αὐτὰ ἐπιτηδεύματα εἶναι ἀνθρώπων πονηρῶν καὶ κακοδαιμόνων; ὁρᾷς ὡς διὰ τούτων οἱονεὶ παραδέχεται μαγείαν εἶναι, οὐκ οἶδα εἰ ὁ αὐτὸς ὢν τῷ γράψαντι κατὰ μαγείας βιβλία πλείονα· πλὴν ὡς χρήσιμον αὐτῷ εἰς τὰ προκείμενα τοῖς ἀπὸ μαγείας ὁμοιοῖ τὰ περὶ Ἰησοῦ ἱστορούμενα. καὶ ἦν ἂν ὅμοια, εἰ μέχρι ἀποδείξεως ὁμοίως τοῖς μαγγανεύουσιν ἔφθανεν δείξας· νυνὶ δὲ οὐδεὶς μὲν τῶν γοήτων δι᾿ ὧν ποιεῖ ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν ἠθῶν ἐπανόρθωσιν καλεῖ τοὺς θεασαμένους οὐδὲ φόβῳ θεοῦ παιδαγωγεῖ τοὺς καταπλαγέντας τὰ θεάματα οὐδὲ πειρᾶται πείθειν οὕτω ζῆν τοὺς ἰδόντας, ὡς δικαιωθησομένους ὑπὸ θεοῦ· καὶ οὐδὲν τούτων ποιοῦσι γόητες, ἐπειδὴ οὐ δύνανται ἢ μηδὲ βούλονται μηδὲ θέλουσι πραγματεύσασθαι τὰ περὶ τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων διορθώσεως, ἅτε καὶ αὐτοὶ πλήρεις ὄντες αἰσχίστων καὶ ἐπιῤῥητοτάτων ἁμαρτημάτων· ὁ δὲ δι᾿ ὧν ἐποίει παραδόξων ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν ἠθῶν ἐπανόρθωσιν τοὺς θεωροῦντας τὰ γινόμενα καλῶν, πῶς οὐκ εἰκὸς ὅτι παρεῖχεν ἑαυτὸν οὐ μόνον τοῖς γνησίοις αὐτοῦ μαθηταῖς ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς παράδειγμα ἀρίστου βίου; ἵνα καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ προτραπῶσιν ἐπὶ τὸ διδάσκειν κατὰ τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ βούλημα τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ πλέον διδαχθέντες ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἢ καὶ τοῦ ἤθους καὶ τῶν παραδόξων, ὡς χρὴ βιοῦν, πάντα πράττωσι κατ᾿ ἀναφορὰν τοῦ ἀρέσκειν τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ. εἰ δὲ τοιοῦτος ἦν ὁ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ βίος, πῶς εὐλόγως ἄν τις αὐτὸν τῇ προαιρέσει τῶν γοήτων παραβάλοι καὶ μὴ κατ᾿ ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ θεὸν εἶναι πιστεύοι ἐν ἀνθρωπίνῳ φανέντα σώματι ἐπ᾿ εὐεργεσίᾳ τοῦ γένους ἡμῶν;
pass_a_gloss: Next after these Celsus, suspecting (ὑπιδόμενος) the great things that will be shown (ἐπιδειχθησόμενα) to have been done by Jesus, of which we have said a few out of many, pretends (προσποιεῖται) to concede (συγχωρεῖν) that true are as many things as are recorded about healings (θεραπειῶν) or resurrection (ἀναστάσεως) or about few loaves having fed many, from which many remnants (λείψανα) were left, or as many other things as he thinks the disciples, making marvels (τερατευσαμένους), have narrated; and he adds to them: 'come, let us believe that these things have been worked by you'. And immediately he puts them in common (κοινοποιεῖ) with the works of sorcerers (γοήτων), as though promising more wonderful things, and with the things performed by those who learned from Egyptians, who in the middle of market-places (ἀγοραῖς) sell (ἀποδομένων) the solemn teachings (σεμνὰ μαθήματα) for a few obols (ὀβολῶν), and drive out (ἐξελαυνόντων) demons from people, and blow away (ἀποφυσώντων) diseases, and call up (ἀνακαλούντων) souls of heroes (ἡρώων), and show costly dinners and tables and cakes (πέμματα) and dishes (ὄψα) that are not, and move as living things (ζῷα) things not truly living but appearing such as far as imagination (μέχρι φαντασίας); and he says: 'then since those do these things, will it be necessary for us to consider them sons of God? Or must it be said that they are practices (ἐπιτηδεύματα) of wicked (πονηρῶν) and ill-fated/demon-ridden (κακοδαιμόνων) men?' You see how through these he as it were (οἱονεί) admits (παραδέχεται) that magic (μαγείαν) exists, I do not know whether being the same as the one who wrote several books against magic; except as useful to him for the matters at hand he likens (ὁμοιοῖ) the things recorded about Jesus to those from magic. And they would be alike, if he had gone as far as display (μέχρι ἀποδείξεως) only, like the conjurers (μαγγανεύουσιν); but now none of the sorcerers through what he does calls the spectators to the correction of characters (ἠθῶν ἐπανόρθωσιν), nor trains (παιδαγωγεῖ) by fear of God (φόβῳ θεοῦ) those astounded (καταπλαγέντας) at the spectacles, nor tries to persuade those who saw to live thus, as those to be justified (δικαιωθησομένους) by God; and sorcerers do none of these, since they cannot, or do not even wish (βούλονται) nor want (θέλουσι) to take in hand (πραγματεύσασθαι) the things about the amendment (διορθώσεως) of humans, inasmuch as themselves being full of the most shameful and most infamous (ἐπιρρητοτάτων) sins (ἁμαρτημάτων); but the one who through the wonders (παραδόξων) he did calls those watching the events to the correction of characters, how is it not likely that he offered himself not only to his genuine (γνησίοις) disciples but also to the rest as an example (παράδειγμα) of the best life? So that both the disciples might be urged (προτραπῶσιν) to teaching humans according to the will (βούλημα) of God, and the rest, taught more (πλέον) from the word (λόγου) or also from the character (ἤθους) and the wonders how one must live, might do everything with reference to (κατ᾽ ἀναφοράν) pleasing (ἀρέσκειν) the God over all (τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ). And if such was the life of Jesus, how reasonably (εὐλόγως) would anyone compare him to the purpose/choice (προαιρέσει) of the sorcerers, and not believe, according to the profession (ἐπαγγελίαν) of being God, him having appeared in a human body for the benefaction (εὐεργεσίᾳ) of our race?
pass_b_english: Next, Celsus, wary of the great works that will be shown to have been done by Jesus, of which we have mentioned a few out of many, pretends to grant that everything recorded is true: the healings, or the raising from the dead, or the few loaves that fed many people and left much over (Matthew 14:17–20), or whatever other marvels he thinks the disciples invented and recorded. And he adds to them: “Come, let us believe that these things were done by you.”

And at once he puts them on a level with the works of sorcerers, as though these promised still more wonderful things, and with the feats performed by those who learned from the Egyptians, who sell their solemn lore for a few obols in the middle of the market-place, drive demons out of people, blow away diseases, call up the souls of heroes, display costly dinners, tables, cakes and dishes that do not exist, and make things move as though they were alive, though they are not truly living things but only appear so to the imagination. And he says: “Since those men do these things, shall we then have to think them sons of God? Or must we say that these are the practices of wicked and wretched men?”

You see how by these words he in effect admits that magic exists. I do not know whether he is the same man who wrote several books against magic. In any case, since it serves his present purpose, he likens what is recorded of Jesus to the works of magic. And they would be alike if Jesus, like the conjurers, had gone no further than a display. But as it is, none of the sorcerers uses what he does to call those who watch to the reform of their characters, nor trains in the fear of God those who are astonished at the spectacle, nor tries to persuade those who saw it to live as people who are to be justified by God. Sorcerers do none of these things, because they cannot, or do not even wish or want to concern themselves with the amendment of human beings, being themselves full of the most shameful and infamous sins.

But he, by the wonders he worked, called those who saw what was happening to the reform of their characters; how, then, is it not likely that he offered himself, not only to his genuine disciples but to the others as well, as an example of the best life? His purpose was that the disciples should be spurred on to teach people according to the will of God, and that the others, taught more fully how one ought to live by his word, or by his character and his wonders as well, should do everything with the aim of pleasing the God who is over all. If such was the life of Jesus, how could anyone reasonably compare him with the sorcerers in their aims, and not believe, as is proclaimed of him, that he is God who appeared in a human body for the good of our race?

choices.choice: The feeding of the many from a few loaves with much left over is told in all four Gospels (Matthew 14:17–20; Mark 6:38–43; Luke 9:13–17; John 6:9–13); Matthew is cited inline as representative. 'The raising from the dead' renders ἀναστάσεως, which Celsus may mean of Jesus' own resurrection or of those he raised; left general. The list of the Egyptian-trained wonder-workers is Origen's indirect report of Celsus, so it is not put in quotation marks; only Celsus's direct words are quoted. κακοδαιμόνων can mean 'wretched' or 'possessed by an evil daemon'; rendered 'wretched'. The writer of 'several books against magic' recalls 1.8, where Origen identifies Celsus with an Epicurean of that name; Origen here doubts the identity. ὡς δικαιωθησομένους ὑπὸ θεοῦ: 'as people who are to be justified by God'; the verb could also mean 'judged', but the positive sense fits the context of moral reform. πλέον διδαχθέντες ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἢ καὶ τοῦ ἤθους καὶ τῶν παραδόξων is taken as 'taught more fully... by his word, and also by his character and his wonders'; it could also be read 'taught more by his word than by his character and wonders'. κατ᾽ ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ θεὸν εἶναι is taken as 'as is proclaimed of him, that he is God' (ἐπαγγελία as profession or announcement), not 'according to the promise'; the Greek does not name who makes the claim, so no subject is supplied. ὑπιδόμενος is rendered 'wary of': Celsus foresees, with suspicion, that Jesus' works will be pointed out. μαγγανεύουσιν is rendered 'conjurers', to keep it apart from γόητες ('sorcerers'). 'The God who is over all' (τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ) is Origen's frequent phrase; it may echo Romans 9:5 but is not a clear allusion, so uncited.

'tales he thinks the disciples told to make a marvel' made 'marvels he thinks the disciples invented and recorded' (τερατευσαμένους ... ἱστορηκέναι)
'like the sorcerers' made 'like the conjurers' (μαγγανεύουσιν, a different word from γόητες)
'because they cannot, and do not even wish' made 'cannot, or do not even wish' (ἢ μηδέ)
Anacoluthon 'But he who ... how is it not likely' made a clean two-part sentence
'by his word, and also by' made 'by his word, or by ... as well' (ἢ καί)
'as he professed' made 'as is proclaimed of him' (κατ᾽ ἐπαγγελίαν); the Greek names no speaker, so none is supplied
